name: Amashsai
title: Priest in Jerusalem after the exile
summary: Amashai was a priest of the family of Immer who settled in Jerusalem after returning from the Babylonian exile. He is mentioned in Neh 11:13 with the lineage Asareel, Achai, and Meshillemoth, which traces back to the priestly family of Immer – one of the 24 priestly divisions established under David. As part of the priestly restoration in Jerusalem, he took part in restoring temple worship, a central task in the post-exilic period. In the parallel genealogy in 1 Chr 9:12, the name form Maasai appears in the corresponding position, which likely refers to the same person or family tradition.

keyEvents.title: Settled among the priests in Jerusalem
keyEvents.description: Amashsai is listed among the priests who settled in Jerusalem after returning from Babylon. He was the son of Azarel, son of Achai, son of Meshillemoth, son of Immer, and thus belonged to one of the prominent priestly families that resumed service in the temple.

keyEvents.title: Service in the rebuilt temple
keyEvents.description: As a priest connected to Immer's priestly division, Amashsai served in worship at God's house in Jerusalem. He was part of a broader group of priests listed in Nehemiah's record of those who settled in the city to maintain the restored temple service.

keyEvents.title: Parallel in Chronicles
keyEvents.description: A parallel genealogy in 1 Chronicles mentions Maasai in a similar position within Immer's lineage. Most scholars regard this as a reference to the same person or tradition, with the name variation due to different transmission lines.

versions.summary: Amasjsai (also known as Amasjai or Amassai) was a priest who settled in Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian exile. He is mentioned in the book of Nehemiah as one of the priests who served in the temple and contributed to the rebuilding of religious life in Jerusalem.

versions.reason: [major] According to Neh 11:13, Amazjai's father is Asarel, but the full lineage is Amazjai son of Asarel, son of Akzai, son of Meshillemot, son of Immer. 'Asarel' as a father ID is acceptable if such an ID exists, but it should be verified that this matches the genealogy in the text. Some translations have 'Azarel' instead of 'Asarel'. This should be checked.; [minor] The description says "son of Asarel," but the full lineage in Neh 11:13 includes several generations (Asarel, Akzai, Meshillemot, Immer). It may be worth including the entire lineage for completeness.; [minor] The event "Rebuilding of religious life" is quite general and not directly tied to a specific event where Amazjai is mentioned. Verses 10–14 cover several priests, not only Amazjai. The event could have been formulated more precisely.; [minor] The description mentions "valiant men" who carried out the work in God's house. This is drawn from Neh 11:14, which refers to another group (the Levites/leaders), not necessarily Amazjai directly. Verse 14 mentions gibborei chayil (valiant or mighty men), but this primarily refers to a different group. This should be clarified.; [minor] The summary is good, but the parenthetical form "(also known as Amazai or Amassai)" may cause confusion with other biblical figures named Amassai (e.g., 1 Chr 12:18). It should be clarified that this refers to name variants of the same person in Neh 11:13.; [minor] Footnotes are missing. A profile should include at least a few footnotes covering linguistic or historical details, such as the meaning of the name, the parallel with 1 Chr 9:12, or the significance of the priestly family of Immer.; [minor] It could be useful to include the parallel passage in 1 Chr 9:12 where the same (or parallel) lineage is mentioned, with some variation in the name forms. BookId 13, chapter 9, verse 12.

The description mixes the context of verses 12–13 (the lineage of Amaziah) with verse 14 (another group). Verse 14 concerns a different priestly/Levitical group under Zabdiel. It is more precise to limit the reference to verses 12–13 or rephrase the description.; [minor] The footnote on priestly rotations is categorized as 'theological', but its content is primarily historical-organizational with an archaeological reference to the Qumran scrolls. footnotes.text: The name Amasjsai (Hebrew: עֲמַשְׁסַי, Amashsai) is a rare name form that occurs only in Neh 11:13. The name may be an abbreviated or altered form of Amaziah ('YHWH bears'). The name form varies in different manuscripts, and the Septuagint has additional variants, suggesting early uncertainty about the exact form.

In 1 Chr 9:12 there is a parallel genealogy where the name Maasai (מַעֲשַׂי) appears in a corresponding position. Many scholars regard Maasai and Amasjsai as variants of the same person or lineage, reflecting different transmission traditions in Hebrew textual history.

The priestly family of Immer was one of the prominent priestly families in Israel. Immer is mentioned as the sixteenth of the 24 priestly divisions established under David (1 Chr 24:14). Descendants of Immer are also mentioned among those who returned from exile (Ezra 2:37), numbering 1,052 people, showing the family's significant size.

The list of priests in Neh 11:10-14 reflects Nehemiah's work to repopulate Jerusalem after the city walls had been rebuilt. According to Neh 11:1-2, lots were cast so that one out of every ten Israelites would settle in the holy city, showing that there was a need for active recruitment to the capital.

The 24 priestly divisions (Hebrew: מִשְׁמָרוֹת, mishmarot) were traditionally organized under King David to ensure a regular rotation system for temple service. This division remained important throughout the entire Second Temple period and is also attested in the Qumran scrolls.
